note: Limits for scripts/bench.py; a run that crosses one exits 1, or 3 when only timings cross on a busy machine. Set on 2026-10-18 from the run at 60f3276 (M-series Mac, 18 cores, load average about 25) plus a margin each 'why' explains. Sizes are measured on the versions uv.lock pins, so their margins are small and a crossing means something was added or the lock moved a dependency (install.installed_mb lists name==version for the biggest). Times are from a shared machine: the same commit measured 9,600 and 14,500 steps/s on the objects-only world at load 30 and 25, so speed limits sit 40 percent under today's numbers and catch gross regressions; when the load is above the cores or objects_20 is under its floor, timings over budget are inconclusive rather than failures. Compare commits with --ab for small changes. Raise a limit only on purpose, with the reason in the commit.

install.wheel_kb.why: 2,547 KB: code, the shipped walk policies and small assets; robot meshes download on first use, so past 4 MB something big got packaged

install.installed_mb.why: 160 MB in a clean venv from uv.lock, mujoco 71 and numpy 20 of it; 20 MB is room for small changes, not for a new heavy dependency

install.download_mb.why: 52.5 MB of wheels from uv.lock for this platform

install.packages.why: 42 distributions; each new one is a decision (docs/GOAL.md approved list)

imports.robotforge_cpu_ms.why: 0.2 ms: the package imports nothing until a command or module needs it (889 ms before, when it loaded the command line)

imports.cli_cpu_ms.why: 596 ms (1,140 before lazy imports): mujoco, uvicorn, the playground and its lessons; +50 percent for a loaded machine

imports.mcp_server_cpu_ms.why: 974 ms (1,268 before): the cli plus the MCP SDK; +45 percent for a loaded machine

imports.robotforge_heavy.why: trimesh, coacd, manifold3d, Pillow and the learning stack load only for the feature that needs them

imports.cli_heavy.why: as above, for every robotforge command

imports.mcp_server_heavy.why: as above, for an agent's session

physics.dog_idle.steps_per_s.why: 69,500 steps/s; 40 percent margin for a shared machine

physics.dog_idle.controllers_share.why: 0.11 of the time in the standing dog's gait (0.28 to 0.31 before the float plan); a regression back toward it crosses 0.18

physics.go2_rl_idle.controllers_share.why: 0.44: the policy network at 50 Hz and its PD loop every step (0.49 to 0.52 before)

physics.humanoid_idle.controllers_share.why: 0.47: a standing humanoid runs its full walking controller (preview control, leg IK) at 100 Hz

physics.warehouse_nav.steps_per_s.why: 3,300 steps/s for a Go2 crossing the warehouse (59 bodies, 294 geoms); 40 percent margin

physics.objects_20.steps_per_s.why: 14,500 to 20,100 steps/s for 20 objects settling on a table at load 11 to 25; no robotforge code in its loop, so it tells how busy the machine was: at 9,500 (load 17 to 23) the humanoid fell under its own floor with no code change. Under 12,000 speed budgets are inconclusive, not failures

physics.dog_idle.peak_mb.why: 160 MB for a process with a dog world

physics.go2_walk.peak_mb.why: 501 to 522 MB: MuJoCo compiling the Go2's OBJ meshes takes about 260 MB of it

viewer.cold_start_s.why: 1.14 s from the command to the first frame with the dog (best of 3; A/B at load 20: 1.22 s before lazy imports, 0.85 s after); wall clock, so a loaded machine needs the margin

viewer.fps.why: 60 fps in headless Chrome, the display rate, on the warehouse with a Go2 at 2560 x 1600

viewer.frame_ms.why: 2.7 to 3.1 ms to draw that frame; 13 ms measured at load 30 with other GPU work

viewer.server_peak_mb.why: 128 MB for the viewer server with a dog world

viewer.idle_cpu_pct.why: 2.6 percent of one core to simulate a standing dog in real time for an open page

mcp.start_s.why: 1.38 s from starting robotforge mcp to its tools listed

mcp.move_ms.why: 33 ms to walk the dog 1 s of simulated time

mcp.idle_cpu_pct.why: 0.4 percent of one core between calls: the simulation clock runs only while the viewer is watched
